subject: Art & Design
title: The Pre-Raphaelites: Medieval Rebels
description: A short lesson to help you apply The Pre-Raphaelites: Medieval Rebels.

hook.text: In 1848, seven young Brits declared war on the entire Royal Academy of Arts.

buildup.text: They called themselves Pre-Raphaelites: they wanted art to return to before Raphael's influence.

discovery.text: They painted with obsessive detail — every leaf, every hair — on a wet white ground for luminosity.

twist.text: Charles Dickens called their work 'revolting.' Critic John Ruskin saved them with a famous defense.

climax.text: Their influence shaped Art Nouveau, the Arts and Crafts movement, and modern fantasy illustration.

punchline.text: They looked backward to push art forward.

quiz.question: What did the Pre-Raphaelites want to return to?
options: Art styles before Raphael's classical influence

details.summary: The Pre-Raphaelite Brotherhood (1848) rejected academic painting's conventions, seeking to return to the vivid color and detail of art before Raphael. Rossetti, Millais, and Hunt painted literary and mythological scenes with jewel-like colors, meticulous natural detail.
details.whyItMatters: The Pre-Raphaelites were the first modern artists' collective to rebel against establishment art. Their influence extends to the Arts and Crafts movement, Art Nouveau, and modern fantasy illustration.
takeaways: Rejected academic conventions to return to pre-Raphael detail
Painted with jewel-like colors and meticulous natural accuracy
Influenced Arts and Crafts, Art Nouveau, and fantasy illustration

faq.question: Why did they reject Raphael specifically?
faq.answer: They saw Raphael as the starting point of academic convention — his idealized compositions became the template that art schools copied endlessly. By going 'before Raphael,' they sought the intense observation and honest emotion of earlier Italian and Flemish painters.

faq.question: What subjects did Pre-Raphaelites typically paint?
faq.answer: Shakespeare, Arthurian legend, Dante, biblical stories, and medieval romance. They also painted contemporary moral subjects with the same intensity. Models posed in historical costumes outdoors, painted with botanical precision against real landscapes.
